newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - British TV giants join forces on digital.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - British TV giants join forces on digital.

text.p: Leading British television companies BSkyB, Carlton Communications and Granada Group said on Friday that they had joined forces to apply to run digital terrestrial TV (DTT) services.
The formation of British Digital Broadcasting, the new venture, appears to transform the prospects for DTT, previously dismissed as a "lame duck" technology.
British Digital Broadcasting has put in an application to run three DTT licences, offering 15 channels.
As well as offering programming from its three members, the venture plans to provide subscription channels from the BBC.
There will be three premium subscription channels showing top Hollywood movies and sporting action. Another 12 channels will be offered as part of a basic subscription package.
DTT will broadcast from land-based transmitters to ordinary rooftop aerials. However, viewers will need a set-top decoder costing at least 200 pounds ($324) to receive it.

There will be six digital networks or "multiplexes", each capable of broadcasting at least five channels. The first two have been earmarked for the existing, free, terrestrial broadcasters, the BBC and the ITV commercial network.
The other four will be awarded by watchdog the Independent Television Commission (ITC). The service is expected to be on the air by mid-1998.
Digital television offers more channels, clearer pictures and the possibility of accessing interactive services such as home shopping and home banking.
But DTT, with only 30 channels, had been seen as the poor relation in comparison with BSkyB's planned satellite version which will offer 200 channels.
BSkyB, in which Rupert Murdoch's News Corp is the leading shareholder, is expected to press on with its digital satellite launch into Britain later this year. DTT is seen as a complementary service.

"By plugging in one simple set top box, viewers will be able to see all the existing terrestrial channels, new free channels, the latest movies and the best sport," said Carlton chairman Michael Green.

Green will chair British Digital Broadcasting, and Carlton, Granada and BSkyB will each own one third of a company which unites Britain's leading commercial ITV companies with satellite pay operator BSkyB.

If successful in winning the three licences, the shareholders have agreed to meet between them a peak funding requirement of up to 300 million pounds. The company is expected to be profitable within five years.
The deadline to apply for digital terrestrial licences is 1200 GMT on Friday. ($1=.6172 Pound)
